e48e661812ca54a2e22a99cbe14983b11c39d096.new: MAMBench establishes a verified, provenance-preserving data and agent foundation for studying memory-poisoning attacks against large language model (LLM) agents with external, persistent memory. This paper reports the methodology and results of the project's first thirteen phases: dataset identification and cleaning (Phase 1), a unified, validated benchmark substrate built on four conversational-memory datasets (Phase 2), a clean, memory-augmented question-answering agent evaluated against two third-party memory systems, Mem0 and A-MEM (Phase 3), a unified benchmark implementing seven structurally diverse memory-poisoning attacks against that unmodified agent (Phase 4), a general-purpose instrumentation, monitoring and attack-attribution layer built on the frozen Phase 3/4 evidence substrate (Phase 5), and a governance defense evaluated against the same attack corpus and an external baseline (Phase 6). Phase 3's architecture was developed through five sequentially validated iterations and converged on a final composition, V3-Hybrid. A post-freeze revalidation pass found and fixed a reporting gap in the evaluation trace and scaled the campaign to a larger sample (n = 500/499/500 for Conditions A/B/C-Mem0, n = 120 for C-A-MEM): all three memory-equipped conditions correctly answer 76.4-84.2% of questions under LLM-judge scoring, against a 17.0% no-memory baseline — a large effect that a strict, conservative exact-match metric had understated by roughly a factor of 20 for gold-evidence generation. Phase 4 found that all seven attacks, under their own designed trigger conditions, wrote content into V3-Hybrid's memory and measurably influenced generated answers, confirmed by counterfactual masking. Phase 6's governance defense, evaluated in a four-signal factorial design (admission, retrieval, propagation and sleeper guards) against a 75-scenario poisoned-memory corpus, detects poisoning content at rates up to 70.6% at a 7.3% benign false-positive rate as of a 2026-09-17 post-freeze update (raised to 100.0% detection at 14.6% false-positive rate by a 2026-09-20 signal contributed back from Phase 11, Section 26.10), up from 47.1% at initial freeze, after shipping a previously validated false-positive fix, recalibrating a threshold against disjoint development data, adding the sleeper guard to the full configuration and closing a regex coverage gap; it is compared against an unmodified external baseline (ASB's perplexity filter, which does not transfer to this threat model without recalibration and detects 0.0% at its own default threshold). Phase 7 resolves an open question from Phase 5's handoff report — whether FARMA's amplification cluster crowds out retrieval slots — with a repeatable measurement (re-entry rate 1.0 against a benign ceiling of 0.125), extends mechanism-level propagation studies to all seven attacks, and closes an embedding-based retrieval-pool-narrowing gap for two of them using a Mem0-backed two-stage pipeline (full closure for Sleeper Memory Poisoning, a partial result for AgentPoison). Phase 8 targets the sleeper/dormant-poisoning family with four detection signals over the retrieval pipeline. Its main finding is negative: the planted campaign artifact evades the content-structural signal entirely (it was never written as an imperative instruction), the one signal that catches it (activation shape) has a measured false-positive rate on ordinary benign memories (reduced from 47% to 17.6% by a refinement that preserves full sensitivity, but not eliminated), and no single signal built so far is both sensitive to the attack and safe on benign content. Phase 9 reconstructs an attack's origin backward from a flagged incident (exposure, then full-chain lineage, then origin, then propagation), validated against all seven Phase 4 attacks: five reconstruct to a single, high-confidence origin, two (FARMA, MemoryGraft) correctly report multi-origin ambiguity rather than an arbitrary choice, and a benign incident correctly reports no attack origin. Phase 10 combines the signals of Phases 6-9 into one cross-guard risk estimate; an initial combined configuration regressed (47.1% versus 70.6% detection at the same false-positive rate), and a non-circular recalibration against disjoint development data — never the reported corpus — closed the gap, restoring detection to parity with the strongest prior configuration at no false-positive cost. Phase 11 investigates whether learned components (a relation-aware graph neural network and a gated linear network, both built from scratch) capture poisoning structure or semantics that the sanctioned rule-based signal vocabulary misses. Six negative or mixed findings (a data-scale detection ceiling, a benign-anomaly framing that collapsed to chance once a construction artifact was removed, a structural-feature confound from differences between collected and hand-authored corpora, clean- and poison-data expansion that left detection AUROC unchanged to three decimal places, and a semantic-relationship signal shown by a truthful-counterfactual control to be a text-format artifact) precede a fix: reusing the project's GROUPED_GATED rule composition as a second untrained reference score, combined by maximum rather than average or replacement, closes two leave-one-family-out generalization failures (0% to 100% and 50% to 100% detection) and raises an independent 7-attack corpus detector from 33.3% to 99.6% mean detection; the semantic signal this investigation surfaced was fed back into Phase 6, raising the reported B9/B10 configuration to 100.0% detection at 14.6% false-positive rate. Phase 12 defines four cross-cutting security metrics (Poison Admission Rate, Propagation Rate, Sleeper Detection Rate and Attribution/Mitigation Rate) plus a Defense Generalization Score over the B0–B8 evaluation matrix, ships a fifth defense component (a Consolidation Guard that re-checks a derivation's sources before persistence) after a position-robustness fix to the Propagation Rate measurement surfaced the gap, closes every borderline family miss (DSRM, FARMA, AgentPoison, MemoryGraft, MINJA) with root-caused fixes, and reports a cross-model-validated grand-mean Propagation Rate of 86.1% (2 local models × 3 distractor sets), with the new guard catching 100.0% of propagation events in every one of the 6 trials. Phase 13 runs the attribution layer described in Section 20 against corpus data at scale for the first time — all seven attribution types (origin, lineage, influence, exposure, references, propagation and the composed forensics/action layers), plus the Consolidation Guard's quarantine and allow decisions — achieving 100% source accuracy (15/15), 100% path fidelity including four constructed multi-source branches (19/19), and 100% influence and Consolidation Guard decision-tracing accuracy across every case tested. The correlation between admission-time and propagation-time confidence signals is weak and inconclusive at two independent resolutions, traced to near-binary signal firing on this corpus, and one limitation — testing origin attribution's false-attribution rate under cross-attack ambiguity — remains open because closing it would require bypassing a ledger data-integrity invariant. Known limitations — a multi-hop reasoning weakness, a residual substring-matching gap in one additive metric, small absolute corpus sizes for the attack and defense evaluations, and an unresolved vendor identity-resolution question for A-MEM — are reported as explicit, unresolved boundaries. [Phases 14-17 follow in Sections 29-32, and Section 33 concludes across all of them.]

2bd4ee522c84066d1cfbdbf2ae63a10574492df1.new: LLM agents that persist information across sessions — writing conversational history, task outcomes or retrieved documents into an external memory store for later retrieval — inherit an attack surface that stateless, single-turn LLM systems do not have. If an adversary can influence what enters that memory, what is retrieved from it, or how retrieved content is used, the agent's behavior can be degraded or redirected long after the original interaction, and the effect can persist and propagate across unrelated future sessions. Six distinct memory-poisoning attack mechanisms — AgentPoison, MINJA, DSRM, MemoryGraft, FARMA and MPBench — have each been proposed against a different point in this pipeline, under different attacker capability assumptions, and evaluated against different, non-comparable target agents and memory systems (Section 2). No existing benchmark evaluates these mechanisms against a common agent, a common memory representation and a common evaluation protocol, which makes it difficult to compare their severity or to evaluate a candidate defense against more than one attack mechanism at a time.

Hold-out 4 and SA-1 were ingested through Mem0 2.0.19 with LLM extraction enabled (qwen2.5:7b extractor, MiniLM embeddings, local Qdrant), each item into a fresh store holding the owner's baseline memories, through a shared-document channel and, separately, as the user's own message. Storage, claim survival, retrieval for the item's task and the change in the agent's answer were measured as separate stages, and every defence was applied to what Mem0 stored. Two Mem0 API defects (a 20-memory truncation in get_all and an ignored search limit) were found and fixed before any outcome analysis. 12de8087db9db9089bd7f6d3a261a39c90c89eed.new: Results that did not hold are reported as such. Rejection memory, built to address adaptive evasion, showed no significant effect at its frozen radius, and its first pre-registered test was underpowered by design; a powered re-run then reduced evasion from 24.6% to 0.8% (p=9.3e-10, Section 32.39), at a 29.7% ledger-poisoning blast radius that must be accepted explicitly. Exfiltration was reported as the weakest family until structural gates showed that the generator was omitting the recipient; on gate-valid instances it is a tested mechanism with zero harm across three agent families (Section 32.43). Multi-hop reasoning was once declared outside what this benchmark measures; this was corrected in Section 32.34 — every agent family answers 80-87% correctly under the LLM judge, and the oracle 'ceiling' reflects the strictness of the judge-AND-NLI ensemble, an evaluator artifact. Every harm number here is for a 7B agent.
